newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Oil rally stemmed after post-Gulf War highs.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Oil rally stemmed after post-Gulf War highs.

text.p: Oil prices shot briefly to post-Gulf War highs early on Tuesday after the United States launched missile attacks against Iraqi defence targets in retaliation for military incursions into the Kurdish safe haven.
October futures for international benchmark Brent blend shot to $23.50 a barrel in Singapore, the highest oil price since shortly after Iraq's invasion of Kuwait six years ago.
But Brent later came back to earth as it became clear there was no threat to Mideast oil supplies outside the loss of imminent Iraqi sales under a U.N. exchange for food.
By 1530 GMT in London Brent was trading at $22.04 a barrel, up five cents, after gains of $1.21 on Monday.
"The fear is that Middle Eastern supplies might be disrupted (but) oil supply is not at significant risk at present," said brokerage Gerald and National Inter Commodities.
Oil traders had been expecting Baghdad in the next few weeks to make its first oil sale on world markets since Gulf War sanctions were imposed six years ago.
But an oil-for-food deal signed in May was suspended by the United Nations on Sunday because of fears for the safety of UN aid distribution monitors in Iraq.
The pact would allow Iraq to sell $2 billion worth of crude over six months, about 550,000 barrels per day (bpd) at current prices, to purchase humanitarian aid for its people.
But Iraqi President Saddam Hussein's latest military adventure had probably derailed the plans for the resumption of Iraqi oil exports beyond the end of the year, oil analysts said.

U.S. envoy to the United Nations Edward Gnehm said the terms of the oil-for-food pact must now be reopened. The eventual timing of Iraqi exports would depend on Baghdad, but could take "months and months," Gnhem said.
"This could delay the oil sale indefinitely because the U.N. can argue they cannot guarantee the safety of the food distributors," said Swiss bank UBS energy analyst Geoff Pyne.
"Perhaps Saddam thought he had nothing to gain by the oil sale so he took a gamble," said Pyne.
"Iraqi oil is not on the agenda until after the U.S. election (in November)," said analyst Charles Gray at London brokerage Prudential Bache.
U.S. defence officials said cruise missiles were fired at military and communications targets in southern Iraq.
Washington extended a "no-fly zone" over safe havens in northern and southern Iraq.
"We're going through a Gulf War instant replay," said Gray at Prudential Bache.
Iraqi Deputy Prime Minister Tareq Aziz said Baghdad would complete a withdrawal of troops from Kurdistan later on Tuesday.
But Saddam declared Western safe havens in Iraq null and void and told his forces to fight back.
Delays to the oil sale came when crude, at $20 for Brent, was already $4 in advance of the same time last year, helped by Middle East tensions and low inventories in the West.
"It's not just missiles that are propelling this market higher, it's panic buying on (petroleum) products," said Gray.
"Those people who thought they would be bailed out by Iraqi oil are now having to rethink things."
Tensions in the region were already high after a truck bomb in Saudi Arabia killed 19 Americans at a military complex in June.
Saudi dissident Osama bin Laden, said to have influenced the Saudi nationals who carried out the attack, called last week for a holy war against U.S. troops in the region.
"Further market-moving attacks are certainly not out of the question and terrorist attacks against U.S. interests may follow," said broker GNI.

"The return of Iraqi oil is very unlikely in 1996. The oil market is going to enter winter with historically low commercial stock levels, the absence of 700,000 barrels per day of Iraqi oil and increased political tension in the Middle East region, which all argues for a fairly tight oil market," said analyst Irene Himona at finance house SG Strauss Turnbull.
